title: How a developer-tool company should write an about page
metaTitle: About pages for a developer-tool company
excerpt: Name who maintains the tool and why that matters to someone about to try it. Skip the origin myth unless it explains a constraint the build still obeys.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The article is about naming the person who actually does the work.
caption: The about page should feel as specific as someone mid-task. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a developer-tool about page prove?
faqs.answer: It should prove that specific people maintain the tool. Name who reviews changes, who handles a security report, and how a stranger reaches a human. A small true team is more believable than a page of silhouettes.

faqs.question: When does an origin story help?
faqs.answer: Keep it when it explains a constraint the product still obeys, such as always showing a raw error. Cut the story that only explains how the founders met or how they felt about the industry. Put any paragraph after the names, and delete it if it would not change a trial.

faqs.question: What should the page ask the reader to do?
faqs.answer: Point them at the try path and give them one check to make in the product. Link a proof page if they want a decision, not only an install. Publish a real contact for security or support, with a response window you will keep.

markdown:
A developer-tool company about page is proof that specific people stand behind the tool. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing wants to know who writes it, who answers when it breaks, and why that should change their decision to try the product. A myth about a garage and a dream does not change that decision.

Skip the origin story unless it explains a constraint the build still obeys. You refused a certain kind of magic because it hid a failure. You still refuse it. That is worth a paragraph. The rest of the biography can wait for a talk. The page has a narrower job.

## Maintainers, not a manifesto

Open with the tool and the people who ship it. What it does, in one sentence you would accept in a README. Who maintains it. How a stranger gets a human when the docs are not enough. You do not need a headcount. You need roles that match the try path. Who reviews the issues. Who is on a security report. Who sits in the call if there is a call.

This reader has met products that were a landing page and a contractor. They are checking whether the bytes have an owner. Answer the check before you offer a worldview. A worldview with no names is a poster. Names with responsibilities are a team, even when the team is two people.

Google's guidance on people-first content treats "who is behind this" as part of whether a page deserves trust. On an about page, that question is the whole assignment. Write so a skeptical reader can repeat who they would be dealing with. If they can only repeat a slogan about empowering developers, the page has joined the marketing they came to escape.

Keep the tone as plain as your docs. Wit is welcome when it is short. Awe is not. They are deciding whether to install something. Match that mood.

## Who does the work

Name the work, then the person or the role. The maintainer who reviews pull requests. The person who handles a security report. The engineer who will look at a migration if you buy the paid help. If the founder still does support, say so. It is a fact, not a humiliation. Hidden scale is what this buyer is trying to detect.

A photo helps when it is a real portrait next to a responsibility. Skip the candid of a hack night that could belong to any company. The sentence under the portrait should say what they own. "Reviews the query planner changes" is a sentence. "Coffee enthusiast" is a different website.

If the company is small, let it look small. Two names and a clear response path are stronger than eight silhouettes. Engineers would rather know the truth before they depend on you in a build. A later surprise about who actually maintains the tool is expensive for them and for you.

Say when outside people do real work. A studio that built the marketing site. A researcher who wrote a design. Hanabi's own public work separates design and build from the client's product. You can be equally plain. Invented staff is a short lie with a long life in a changelog, where the same three names keep appearing.

Use the titles they will hear. Maintainer. Support. Founder, if the founder is in the work. Decorative titles with no verb should come off the page. If a title has no responsibilities under it, cut the title.

Say how a change ships. Who can merge. Who writes the migration note. Who is allowed to call a bug a break. An engineer reading the about page is imagining the week after they depend on you. A name without a merge right is a mascot. A name with a merge right is an answer. You do not need to publish the on-call rota. You do need the reader to believe a rota exists and that a person owns it. If the honest version is "the founder still merges," write that. It is a better signal than a chart of future departments.

## Why this reader should care

Relevance is a practice they can test after they try the product. You answer issues with a reproduction, or you say you cannot. You mark breaking changes in the changelog with the version and the fix. You keep a migration note when you move a default. Pick practices that are true. Describe one of them in a few sentences.

Connect the practice to the screen they saw on the homepage. If the tool comments on a risky migration, the about page can say who writes those rules and how a false positive gets removed. The homepage showed the mechanism. This page shows the owner of the mechanism. Together they feel like a tool with a maintainer, which is the bar.

Skip values that any company can print. Integrity. Passion. Excellence. If a value is operational, state the operation. "A security report gets a human reply from a named address, and we do not ask you to file it as a feature request." That can be checked. The abstract word cannot.

Leave awards and user counts off unless you would defend them in a GitHub thread. This buyer enjoys finding a soft number. Give them fewer chances. A single practice, visible in the product, will do more than a badge.

## When the origin earns a paragraph

Keep an origin story when it locks a constraint they will feel in the try. You started the tool because a log tool hid the raw line, and you still show the raw line even when a summary exists. That story tells them what you will not "improve" away. It changes how they evaluate the product.

Cut the story that only explains how the founders met, what they studied, or how frustrated they were with the industry. Frustration with the industry is the default origin of every developer tool. It does not distinguish you. The constraint does.

If you keep the paragraph, put it after the names and the practice. End it on the present behavior of the tool. A story that stays in the past asks them to trust a memory. They would rather trust a default they can toggle today.

Apply one test. Would this paragraph change whether they try the product, or change what they look for when they try it? If it would not, delete it. The page gets shorter and more serious, which is the right direction for this audience.

## What to leave out

Leave the childhood and the conference-circuit travelogue. Leave a quote about changing how the world builds software. Leave a wall of technology logos as a personality. A line about the runtime can stay if it matters. "The agent runs in your CI, not on a laptop we control." That is a reason. A sticker sheet of clouds is not.

Leave the customer quote you wrote for them. Leave the headcount you hope to have next year. The about page is easy to forward. Every sentence should survive a forward to a staff engineer who did not want to be impressed.

Leave the hard close that pretends the memoir was the product. The action is to try the tool. The about page can point at that action once the people are clear. It should not pivot into a pitch that abandons the names you just earned.

## Point them at the try path

Close by sending them to try the product, and tell them what the about page changed. They know who will answer if the trial breaks. They know one practice to look for. Suggest a concrete check. "See whether the raw error is still visible after the summary." A page that offers a check is speaking their language.

Keep a second step for the reader who wants judgment, not only a trial. Link to a proof page. One constraint, one decision, the real screen. The about page is the people. The proof page is the choice. They support each other, and neither replaces the install.

If you publish a security contact or a support address, put it here in full, with the response you actually give. "A person replies on business days." Ordinary language. Do not promise a minute you have not staffed. An engineer will test the address the way they test an API. Be the document, not the campaign.

## A page you can ship

Build it in this order.

1. The tool, in a README sentence, and the buyer it is for.
2. Who maintains it, tied to issues, security, and the trial.
3. One practice they can test after they install.
4. A constraint you still obey, with a short origin only if it explains the constraint.
5. What you will not claim.
6. Try the product, plus the check you invited them to make.

Read it as if you were about to give the tool permission to run in CI. Do you know who owns a breaking change? Do you know how to reach them? If the answer is a slogan, replace the slogan with a name, a role, or a cut. Warmth will not patch a missing owner.

People make the tool believable. A record of a hard choice makes the people believable. Read [what a proof page should show an engineer](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-developer-tool-company) before you add another personal essay.

For a look at work presented as decisions rather than as a mood, see [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The about page should be able to stand next to that kind of evidence.
